name: Nora Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on my mum and dad's farm, Hillcrest, up on the hill road. We've got five hundred ewes, thirty hectares of potatoes and a bit of oats. This time of year it's tupping, which is when the rams go in with the ewes, so I'm round the flock on the quad bike first thing with the dogs, Moss and Jen, checking the raddle marks. Then potatoes in store need turning and checking, and there's always a gate to hang or a wall down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like beyond the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Daniel, he's a mechanic at the tractor dealer in town, and we're getting married at the chapel next August. We live in the old farm cottage, which Dad lets us have cheap, and I've got about four months' wages put by, most of it meant for the wedding. Dad pays me a proper wage, same as he'd pay anyone. I don't use any of the AI things; I've no need, and I don't trust what I can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Most of what we're told is coming never comes, and farming carries on because people need feeding. I'd say it at church, maybe, or at the livestock market in town, not on the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. It's another of those things the city people get excited about that doesn't change a thing on a hill farm. My granddad farmed this hill, my dad farms it, and I'd like to be the one after him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the same. Keep saving for the wedding, keep the flock, and maybe push Dad to grow a bit more of the early potatoes, because they've been paying well. Nothing to do with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's how it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust what you can't see. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I buy a ewe, I look at her feet, her teeth, her udder. You can see what you're getting. With those AI things, you're trusting somebody in an office somewhere who's never seen a sheep, and I'd rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad think about all the talk around AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He laughs at it, mostly. He's got a phone that flips open and he only answers it if it's the auction. He says the day a computer can find a ewe stuck in a ditch in the snow, he'll retire. I'd say that's about right.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because most of what we're told is coming never comes and people still need feeding. I'd say it at church or the livestock market, not online.
S0.think: I'd be glad it's another city excitement that changes nothing on a hill farm. My granddad and my dad farmed this hill, and I'd like to be the one after him.
S0.do: Carries on the same, saving for her wedding and keeping the flock. Pushes her father to grow more early potatoes because they've been paying well, with no new technology involved.
S0.quote: With those AI things, you're trusting somebody in an office somewhere who's never seen a sheep, and I'd rather not.
S0.fieldNote: Nora's sense of security comes from family continuity on the land and a strong distrust of things she can't inspect herself. She frames AI as a city enthusiasm. Her father's flip phone and his snowbound-ewe test sum up the family's view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms like ours will be fine, it's the big ones that'll change. I'd also say the government should keep out of it, not pay people to sit at home. If people need new skills, then teach them a trade, apprenticeships, proper work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the potatoes worry me a bit. There are already machines that grade potatoes with cameras, and Daniel says the dealer's been selling them. If the big growers go robot and the price drops, our thirty hectares won't pay, but the sheep on the hill, no robot's doing those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as we are and see. I'd keep the wedding money and save a bit more on top. If the potatoes stopped paying, I'd tell Dad we should drop them and do more sheep, maybe sell lamb straight to people ourselves. But I wouldn't be buying any of the new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it would be on my mind when I'm turning the potatoes in the store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Daniel works at the dealer selling these machines. Does that cause any tension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, at Sunday dinner. Dad will say, your lot are putting farmers out of work, and Daniel will say, somebody's got to fix them when they break, and they always break. It's mostly joking. Mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if the potatoes stopped paying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets, first, because they squeeze us already. And the big companies who make these machines and sell them like miracles. Not the farmers who buy them, they've got bills same as us.

S1.say: I'd say farms like ours will be fine and it's the big ones that will change. The government should stay out of it and teach people trades through apprenticeships, not pay them to sit at home.
S1.think: The potatoes worry me, because camera graders already exist and robot growers could push the price down until our thirty hectares don't pay. But no robot is doing the sheep on the hill.
S1.do: Keeps going as before and saves a little on top of the wedding fund. If potatoes stop paying, urges her father to drop them and sell lamb directly to customers, without buying any new machines.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not losing sleep but thinking about it while she turns potatoes in the store.
S1.quote: Dad will say, your lot are putting farmers out of work, and Daniel will say, somebody's got to fix them when they break, and they always break.
S1.fieldNote: Nora separates the exposed potato side from the sheep, which she sees as safe. Her views are clear: apprenticeships and trades, not support payments. Her fiancé selling and fixing the machines brings the issue to the family table in a joking but tense way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let a handful of tech companies decide everything. People should stand up for their own work and their own land. I'd vote for whoever wanted to protect farms and family businesses, and I'd say so at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it would frighten me. If machines can do everything in two years, including the hill work, then a big company could buy up farms and run them with robots and nobody living there. Our farm would still be ours, but what's it worth if lamb and potatoes are cheaper from a robot farm than we can grow them?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, we'd cut back the wedding, a smaller party in the chapel hall, not the hotel. I'd sit down with Mum and Dad and work out what Hillcrest could live on, maybe fewer sheep and selling direct. We'd lean on each other, and on the chapel, because that's what they're for. I wouldn't be learning to use robots, I'll say that now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground moving under the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel about the wedding being smaller?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I don't care about the hotel, I care about him and the chapel. He'd be relieved, honestly, he hates a fuss. The hard one would be telling my mum, who's had the menu planned since I was ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn to use robots. Even if it meant keeping the farm going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about that, and I don't know. If it was that or losing Hillcrest, maybe Daniel could run them and I'd keep the sheep. But I'd feel like I was handing the farm to the very thing that's ruining it.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when a handful of tech companies decide everything, and people should stand up for their own work and land. I'd vote for whoever protects farms and family businesses.
S2.think: It would frighten me, because big companies could run farms with robots and nobody living there. Our farm would still be ours, but it wouldn't be worth much if robot farms grew lamb and potatoes cheaper than we can.
S2.do: Cuts the wedding back to a smaller event in the chapel hall and works out with her parents what the farm could live on, with fewer sheep and direct sales. Leans on family and the chapel, and refuses to learn to use robots herself.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the ground moving under the farm.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I was handing the farm to the very thing that's ruining it.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario threatens Nora's whole way of life, not just her wage. Her response leans on family, chapel and voting rather than retraining. She wavers only when asked whether she'd accept robots to save the farm, and then pictures her fiancé running them while she keeps the sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for farming families to stand together and get ready. I'd say sell your own produce, build your own customers, and don't wait for the government. At church I'd say the same about looking after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's still bad for farms like ours, but we'd have a chance to build something people want because a person made it. Proper lamb from a hill farm, with a name on it. Some people will pay for that, I think, though I can't be sure how many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years I'd start selling lamb boxes direct, maybe to forty families to start, from a freezer in the old dairy. I'd keep saving, and we'd go ahead with the wedding but keep it simple. Daniel's offered to set up a website for the lamb boxes, and that's as close to computers as I'd get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But with something to work on, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would a lamb box sell for, and would it pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half a lamb, butchered and packed, maybe eighty to a hundred. Forty boxes a year isn't a living, but with the sheep and Dad's land, it'd help. If it grew to a hundred and fifty, that's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said that's as close to computers as you'd get. What if the website needed AI to keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Daniel can do it. He likes all that. I'll do the sheep and talk to the customers, which I'm good at, and he can do the clicking.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for farming families to stand together and get ready: sell your own produce, build your own customers, and don't wait for the government.
S3.think: It's still bad for farms like ours, but there'd be time to build something people want because a person made it, like hill lamb with a name on it. Some people will pay for that, though I can't say how many.
S3.do: Starts selling half-lamb boxes direct to about forty families from a freezer in the old dairy, priced around eighty to a hundred each. Keeps saving, holds a simple wedding, and lets her fiancé build and run the website.
S3.feel: Anxious, but helped by having something to work on.
S3.quote: I'll do the sheep and talk to the customers, which I'm good at, and he can do the clicking.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Nora turns to self-reliance: selling direct and building a name, which fits her free-market and family values. She is honest that she doesn't know how many customers would pay for human-raised lamb. She divides the work clearly, keeping technology with her fiancé.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say farming families have time to plan, so let's not cry about it. I'd say what my granddad said: make hay while the sun shines. And I'd say the young ones should learn a real trade, not just a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd find a way. Ten years is long enough to build the lamb boxes up, and maybe a farm shop, and for Daniel to do well fixing robots, which I'll admit someone has to. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with children, and I'd want them to grow up on Hillcrest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the lamb boxes in a year or two and grow them steadily. We'd go ahead with the proper wedding next August, and over the years put money into a small farm shop at the end of the lane, maybe ten thousand, mostly from family. I'd keep the flock and let the potatoes go when they stop paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's a long way off and we've got the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned children growing up on Hillcrest. What would that look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them out on the hill with the dogs like I was, knowing a sick ewe by how she stands. Maybe there'd be robots in the potato field by then, but I'd want them knowing the sheep themselves. That's not something you learn from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never use robots, but you admit Daniel might fix them. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it is. I don't mind other people using them, it's their farm. I just don't want my life to be about them. If Daniel makes a good living out of it, well, that keeps us on the hill too.

S4.say: I'd say farming families have time to plan, so let's not cry about it, and make hay while the sun shines. Young people should learn a real trade, not just a computer.
S4.think: I think we'd find a way, with time to build lamb boxes and a farm shop and for my fiancé to do well fixing robots. At thirty-seven, maybe with children, I'd want them to grow up on the farm.
S4.do: Starts lamb boxes within a year or two and grows them steadily, goes ahead with the full wedding, and over the years puts about ten thousand, mostly from family, into a farm shop. Keeps the flock and drops the potatoes once they stop paying.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady, with the land beneath her.
S4.quote: I'd want them out on the hill with the dogs like I was, knowing a sick ewe by how she stands.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Nora keep her wedding and plan a family on the farm, and her worry drops a level. She accepts the contradiction of disliking robots while relying on her fiancé's work fixing them. The land is her real cushion.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to build anything; you'd just watch it happen. What would help is rules that stop big companies buying up farms to run with robots, and help for family farms to sell direct, like a local market that's properly supported. Not handouts, just a fair chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: What happens to the villages. If the farms go to companies, there's nobody in the chapel on Sunday, nobody at the school gate. Machines don't come to funerals. That's what I'd want someone to think about.

portrait: Nora Reyes is 27 and works for a wage on her parents' hill farm, Hillcrest, looking after 500 ewes and 30 hectares of potatoes. She lives in the old farm cottage with her fiancé Daniel, a mechanic at the tractor dealer, and is saving for their chapel wedding next August. She has never used AI and distrusts anything she can't see and check herself. Her worry rises with speed: calm in a plateau, uneasy about potato prices in steady change, and alarmed by two-year AGI, which she sees as a threat to her family's way of life. Given five or ten years, she plans to sell lamb direct, open a farm shop and raise children on the hill, while leaving the technology to Daniel.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because there'd be no time to build anything and she'd just watch the farm's value collapse.
whatWouldHelp: Rules stopping big companies from buying up farms to run with robots, and support for family farms to sell directly through properly supported local markets, not handouts.
